object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer as tracked by the billing system; everything hangs off this.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: Account Number
object_types.definition: Six digit, sequential, never-reused identifier of an account.

source_references.excerpt: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.
Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: Price Plan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what a customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: Feature Bundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle a customer gets -- seats, API access, SSO -- identified by name; what's on the pricing page.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: Start Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Subscription ID. The account. The product. The price plan. Start date. End date, sometimes. Billing period. Status.

object_types.name: End Date
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends, if fixed-term or cancelled; optional.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: Billing Period
object_types.definition: The cycle on which a subscription is billed.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: Subscription Status
object_types.definition: The lifecycle status of a subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: Paused Flag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean indicating a subscription is paused; not part of the status enumeration, overlaps confusingly with active status.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan and billing period, not stored on the subscription in the source system.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue. It's the number I live in.
It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83.

object_types.name: Plan Change
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with an effective date and requester; the objectification of the plan change relationship.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: Effective Date
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for at least three distinct concepts in the business: Priya's 'price plan' (billing artefact), Tom's 'feature bundle' (what customer gets, called 'plan' on the pricing page), and a third 'plan' used by sales referring to the negotiated deal, which frequently matches neither of the other two. The transcript only fully resolves the relationship between the first two; the sales usage is explicitly not modeled.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan. ... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.
Only that we still call three different things "plan" and this document won't fix that.

ambiguities.description: Whether the 'one active subscription per account per product' rule is enforced via a uniqueness constraint scoped to 'active-like' statuses (active, trialing, past due?) or literally only the 'active' status is unclear -- the paused flag overlap makes the definition of 'active' ambiguous for constraint purposes.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term, prorated refund, or credit) is explicitly undecided and parked; only the current system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund mechanism) is captured, not a business rule.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided. The model will capture the system behaviour... and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: It is unclear whether 'account' and 'company/customer' are truly identical concepts for product purposes -- Tom notes that when an account closes and the same company returns, they get a new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting, losing history. This suggests 'Account' and 'Company' may be distinct concepts not fully modeled (no Company object type was introduced).

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.
Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history.

ambiguities.description: Whether feature bundle names/count are a fixed closed set (like the four statuses) or just the currently known set is unclear -- unlike products and statuses, no one explicitly says bundles are fixed at three, though only three are named.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

ambiguities.description: The final exchange reveals that the subscription's 'current price plan' is a denormalised, derived-but-stored field maintained by the change process, distinct from the plan change history. It's ambiguous whether this current-plan field should be modeled as a genuine stored fact (with its own mandatory/uniqueness constraints) or as a pure derivation like MRR, since Priya insists it 'does have a current plan field' but concedes it is 'maintained by the change process' and that if it disagrees with history, 'the change history wins and the current plan is the bug' -- implying it's an unreliable cache rather than an authoritative fact.

source_references.excerpt: It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for. The subscription's plan at any moment is derived. No, Sam, it does have a current plan field.
Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: The four manual credits/refunds issued 'outside the subscription' for mid-term cancellations are not modeled as a fact type since they are explicitly goodwill/manual actions rather than a system rule; it's unclear whether these should eventually be captured as a distinct 'Refund' or 'Credit' concept once the business rule is decided.

source_references.excerpt: It becomes one when the customer escalates and we give them a refund anyway, which we did four times last quarter.
the four Tom's talking about were manual credits raised outside the subscription
